title: Babbage, Lovelace and the idea of a programmable engine
text:
CHAPTER 1. LOGIC BEFORE MACHINES
SECTION 1.3. BABBAGE, LOVELACE AND THE IDEA OF A PROGRAMMABLE ENGINE

Boole gave us the mathematics of logic. Frege and Hilbert asked whether reasoning could be mechanized. But long before either question was posed precisely, an English mathematician tried to build mechanical computers out of brass gears. Charles Babbage never finished his machines, but his designs contain, a century early, most of the architecture of a modern computer: a processor, a memory, input and output, and conditional branching. Ada Lovelace, writing about his design, produced the first published discussion of what such a machine might and might not be able to do, a discussion Alan Turing would answer directly in 1950.

1. The problem: tables full of errors

In the early nineteenth century, science, navigation, engineering, finance and insurance depended on printed tables: logarithms, trigonometric functions, astronomical positions, interest rates. These were computed by hand by human "computers," checked, typeset and printed, and errors could enter at every stage. A navigator using a wrong value could lose a ship.

Charles Babbage (1791-1871), a Cambridge-trained mathematician, became convinced that tables should be calculated and typeset by machine. In about 1821 he and his friend John Herschel were checking astronomical tables computed by hand for the Astronomical Society and found many discrepancies. In an account Babbage wrote in 1839, he recalled exclaiming, "I wish to God these calculations had been executed by steam," to which Herschel replied, "It is quite possible." (Babbage's earlier accounts of 1822 and 1834 describe the same episode in slightly different words, so treat the exact phrasing as his later recollection.)

2. The Difference Engine and the method of finite differences

Babbage's first design, the Difference Engine, was a special-purpose calculator. Its central trick is the method of finite differences, which lets you tabulate any polynomial using only addition. This is worth working through, because it is a lovely example of turning a hard operation into a simple, repeatable mechanical one.

Take the polynomial f(x) = x^2 + x + 41. Compute a few values and their differences:

    x    f(x)    1st diff    2nd diff
    0     41
                    2
    1     43                    2
                    4
    2     47                    2
                    6
    3     53                    2
                    8
    4     61

For a polynomial of degree n, the n-th differences are constant. Here degree is 2, and every second difference is 2. So once you know the starting value f(0) = 41, the first difference 2 and the constant second difference 2, you can generate the whole table by additions alone:

    next 1st diff = current 1st diff + 2nd diff
    next f        = current f + current 1st diff

Mechanically, the engine holds a column of number wheels for f, one for the first difference, one for the second difference, and so on. Each cycle adds each column into the one above it. No multiplication is needed. Functions that are not polynomials (like logarithms) can be approximated piecewise by polynomials, so the method covers most practical tables.

Babbage built a small demonstration piece and in the 1820s obtained British government funding for a full Difference Engine (now called Difference Engine No. 1). The engineer Joseph Clement did much of the precision machining. The project ran into cost overruns, a dispute between Babbage and Clement, and loss of government confidence, and it stopped in the early 1830s with only a portion assembled. That surviving portion is held by the Science Museum in London.

Babbage later designed an improved, simpler Difference Engine No. 2 (designed in the late 1840s). He never built it. Between 1985 and 1991 the Science Museum in London built one from his drawings, and it worked, which settled the old question of whether Babbage's designs were buildable with the precision available to the period. A printer mechanism designed by Babbage was completed afterwards. A second copy was built for a private owner and was exhibited for several years at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, California.

3. The Analytical Engine: a general-purpose design

While the Difference Engine project was faltering, Babbage conceived a far more ambitious machine, the Analytical Engine, beginning around 1834 and refining it for the rest of his life. It was never built, beyond small trial pieces, but it is the first design for a general-purpose, program-controlled computer.

Its architecture, in modern terms:

  The Store. A memory of numbers held on columns of decimal wheels. Babbage's plans contemplated on the order of a thousand numbers of about forty or fifty decimal digits each (figures vary by design version). This is the analogue of RAM.

  The Mill. The arithmetic unit, able to add, subtract, multiply and divide. Numbers were moved from the store to the mill, operated on, and returned. This is the analogue of the CPU's ALU and registers. The words "store" and "mill" were Babbage's, and the separation of memory from processor is the same separation found in the later von Neumann architecture (Section 4.4).

  Punched cards for control. Babbage borrowed the idea from the Jacquard loom, which since the early 1800s had used chains of punched cards to control the pattern woven into fabric. In the Analytical Engine, separate card types specified operations (operation cards) and which store locations to use (variable cards), and number cards could supply constants. This is the program, held externally rather than in the store.

  Output. A printer, a curve plotter and a card punch for results were contemplated.

  Conditional control. Crucially, the design allowed the sequence of cards to be advanced or backed up depending on a result, for instance on the sign of a number. This is a conditional branch, and with it loops. A machine with arithmetic, memory and conditional branching on stored results is, given enough memory, capable in principle of any computation, which in Turing's later language makes it "universal" (Section 3.2). Historians generally describe the Analytical Engine as Turing-complete in design, with the usual caveat that real memory is finite.

It is worth noticing what the Analytical Engine did not have. It was decimal, not binary. It was mechanical, driven by cranks and (in plan) steam, so it would have been slow, so even simple operations would have taken seconds. And its program lived on cards outside the store; the idea of putting instructions in the same memory as data, and letting the program modify itself, came only in the 1940s.

4. Ada Lovelace and the Notes

Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (1815-1852), was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron and Annabella Milbanke. Her mother had her educated in mathematics and science, and she met Babbage in 1833, when she was seventeen, and became interested in his engines.

In 1842 the Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea (later a Prime Minister of Italy) published, in French, an account of the Analytical Engine based on lectures Babbage gave in Turin. Lovelace translated it into English and, at Babbage's suggestion, added her own notes, labeled A through G. The notes turned out to be roughly three times as long as the original article. The translation with notes was published in 1843 under her initials, A.A.L.

Note G contains a detailed table showing how the Analytical Engine could compute the Bernoulli numbers, a sequence important in number theory and analysis. The table lists, step by step, which operations the mill performs, which variables in the store are read and written, and how a group of operations is repeated. It is often called the first published computer program. Historians debate how much of the work was Lovelace's own and how much came from Babbage; Babbage wrote that he supplied the formulas and that Lovelace caught a mistake of his. Modern re-implementations of the table have found a bug in it: two variables are swapped in one division, so run exactly as printed it would give a wrong value for the last Bernoulli number computed. Even so, the notes are clearly written in Lovelace's voice and show genuine understanding of the machine.

Her notes are remembered for two broader ideas.

Generality beyond numbers. Lovelace argued that the engine operated on symbols that could stand for things other than quantities. She suggested that if the relations of musical sounds could be expressed in this way, the engine might compose elaborate pieces of music. This is a striking early statement that a computing machine is a general symbol manipulator, not just a calculator, which is the core assumption of symbolic AI a century later.

The limitation. Lovelace also wrote, in Note G, that the Analytical Engine "has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform." This is the most famous sentence in the notes. In his 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," Turing discussed this as "Lady Lovelace's Objection" and replied, among other points, that machines can surprise us and that a learning machine might come to do things its programmer did not foresee (Section 8.1). The debate about whether machines can be creative, revived by every generation of AI up to today's generative models, started here.

5. Why Babbage's engines were not built, and why it mattered

Explanations historians give for the failure include: the high cost of precision manufacturing in the period; Babbage's tendency to redesign continually rather than freeze a design; disputes with his engineer; lack of a clear funding customer for a general-purpose machine; and his difficult relations with the government. The 1991 Science Museum construction showed that the mechanical precision was not the fatal obstacle for the Difference Engine.

Babbage's ideas had limited direct influence on the builders of the first electronic computers. Howard Aiken, designer of the Harvard Mark I (Section 2.4), did know of Babbage's work and acknowledged him. But most of the 1940s pioneers rediscovered the key concepts independently from the needs of their own problems and from the theory of Turing and others. The lesson for engineers is sobering: a correct architectural idea can wait a century for its enabling technology. The Analytical Engine needed fast, reliable, cheap switching elements. Those arrived first as relays, then as vacuum tubes, then as transistors, which is the story of Chapters 2, 4 and 5.

6. Mechanical computing in between

Mechanical calculating machines did not disappear after Babbage. Before him, Blaise Pascal (1640s) and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1670s onward) had built adding and multiplying calculators; Leibniz also wrote about binary arithmetic and dreamed of a universal logical calculus, a "calculus ratiocinator," an idea that anticipates both Boole and AI. Through the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries mechanical desk calculators became common office equipment.

Another important line was punched-card data processing. Herman Hollerith built electromechanical tabulating machines that read punched cards with electrical contacts, used to process the 1890 United States census. His company later became part of the firm that was renamed IBM in 1924. Punched cards, which came from looms via Babbage and Hollerith, remained the main input medium for computers into the 1970s.

Analog computing was also important. Lord Kelvin's tide-predicting machines of the 1870s and Vannevar Bush's differential analyzer at MIT, completed around 1931, solved differential equations with rotating shafts and mechanical integrators. Bush's machine has a direct connection to our next chapter: Claude Shannon worked on the differential analyzer as a graduate student at MIT, and the complex relay control circuit of the analyzer helped inspire his 1937 thesis on switching circuits (Section 2.1).

7. Engineering takeaways

  - Reduce hard operations to repeated simple ones. The method of differences replaces polynomial evaluation by addition, just as later hardware reduces multiplication to shifts and adds.
  - Separate memory from processing, and control from data. Store, mill and cards correspond to memory, ALU and program.
  - Conditional branching is what turns a calculator into a general computer.
  - A design is only as good as its enabling technology and its project management.

8. Summary

  - Babbage's Difference Engine (1820s-1830s) tabulated polynomials by the method of finite differences using only addition; it was never completed in his lifetime, but Difference Engine No. 2 was built from his plans by the Science Museum, London, and worked.
  - The Analytical Engine (designed from about 1834) had a store, a mill, punched-card programs adapted from the Jacquard loom, and conditional branching: the first general-purpose computer design.
  - Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes included a step-by-step procedure for computing Bernoulli numbers, argued the machine could manipulate any symbols, and stated that it could not "originate anything," an objection Turing answered in 1950.
  - The key concepts had to wait for electrical switching technology, the subject of the next chapter.
